claim: RNA viruses typically have high mutation rates, resulting in frequent production of protein variants with compromised biophysical properties.
source: RNA viruses typically have high mutation rates, resulting in frequent production of protein variants with compromised biophysical properties.
evidence: This is a general statement about RNA viruses supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Host proteostasis mechanisms are significant determinants of the fitness of viral protein variants, serving as a critical force shaping viral evolution.
source: We hypothesized that host proteostasis mechanisms may be significant determinants of the fitness of viral protein variants, serving as a critical force shaping viral evolution.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, tested through experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both the nature of selection on the influenza genome and the accessibility of specific mutational trajectories are significantly impacted by host proteostasis.
source: We find that both the nature of selection on the influenza genome and the accessibility of specific mutational trajectories are significantly impacted by host proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from serial passaging experiments and sequencing analysis presented in Figures 3-6.

claim: Most missense mutations have deleterious consequences for protein function, often owing to either thermodynamic or kinetic effects on folding.
source: Most missense mutations have deleterious consequences for protein function, often owing to either thermodynamic (reduced stability of the native state or enhanced stability of unfolded/misfolded states) or kinetic (slow folding or enhanced misfolding/aggregation) effects on folding (DePristo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DePristo et al., 2005.

claim: The distribution of mutational fitness effects in viruses can be largely accounted for by considering protein folding biophysics.
source: In the context of viruses, these phenomena may underpin the observation that the distribution of mutational fitness effects can be largely accounted for by considering protein folding biophysics (Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; Chéron et al., 2016; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; Chéron et al., 2016; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009a.

claim: Stable proteins tend to be more evolvable, as any given missense mutation is less likely to severely disrupt protein folding or structure.
source: Indeed, stable proteins tend to be more evolvable, as any given missense mutation is less likely to severely disrupt protein folding or structure (Bloom et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bloom et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2013.

claim: Proteostasis networks are composed of chaperones and quality control factors that work in concert to shepherd nascent proteins to folded, functional conformations.
source: In cells, protein folding challenges are addressed by proteostasis networks composed of chaperones and quality control factors that work in concert to shepherd nascent proteins to folded, functional conformations (Balch et al., 2008; Hartl et al., 2011; Powers and Balch, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balch et al., 2008; Hartl et al., 2011; Powers and Balch, 2013.

claim: Hsp90 chaperone plays a critical role in modulating the evolution of its endogenous clients.
source: Important work focused primarily on the Hsp90 chaperone has suggested a critical role for chaperones in modulating the evolution of their endogenous clients, (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Queitsch et al., 2002; Lachowiec et al., 2015; Sangster et al., 2007, 2008a, 2008b; Rohner et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2014; Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2016; Rutherford and Lindquist, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on Hsp90.

claim: Hsp90 activity can buffer deleterious effects of non-synonymous mutations.
source: Important work focused primarily on the Hsp90 chaperone has suggested a critical role for chaperones in modulating the evolution of their endogenous clients, (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Queitsch et al., 2002; Lachowiec et al., 2015; Sangster et al., 2007, 2008a, 2008b; Rohner et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2014; Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2016; Rutherford and Lindquist, 1998) in part by buffering deleterious effects of non-synonymous mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Hsp90.

claim: Hsp90-dependent azole resistance in Candida albicans is mediated by secondary effects of Hsp90 on calcineurin.
source: For instance, Hsp90-dependent azole resistance in Candida albicans is mediated by secondary effects of Hsp90 on calcineurin, an Hsp90 client that regulates responses to environmental stimuli (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cowen and Lindquist, 2005.

claim: The GroEL/ES chaperonin system can govern the fitness of certain client protein variants in bacteria.
source: However, Tawfik and coworkers have shown that the GroEL/ES chaperonin system can govern the fitness of certain client protein variants in bacteria (Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009b.

claim: Computational modeling suggests that chaperones other than Hsp90 may have roles in evolution.
source: and computational modeling suggests that other chaperones may also have roles in evolution (Bogumil and Dagan, 2012; Cetinbaş and Shakhnovich, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bogumil and Dagan, 2012; Cetinbaş and Shakhnovich, 2013.

claim: Most RNA viruses lack autonomous chaperones or other co-factors to assist their proteins with folding.
source: Intriguingly, most RNA viruses lack autonomous chaperones or other co-factors to assist their proteins with folding.
evidence: This is a general statement about RNA viruses supported by established knowledge in virology.

claim: Viral proteins engage host chaperones.
source: Instead, viral proteins engage host chaperones, (Melville et al., 1999; Momose et al., 2002; Naito et al., 2007; York et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Melville et al., 1999; Momose et al., 2002; Naito et al., 2007; York et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2010.

claim: Host chaperone inhibitors have been shown to limit the viability of certain RNA viruses.
source: and host chaperone inhibitors have been shown to limit the viability of certain RNA viruses (Geller et al., 2007; Heaton et al., 2016; Taguwa et al., 2015; Chase et al., 2008; Geller et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Geller et al., 2007; Heaton et al., 2016; Taguwa et al., 2015; Chase et al., 2008; Geller et al., 2012.

claim: The possibility that host chaperones can shape the evolution of viral pathogens has not been investigated prior to this work.
source: However, the possibility that host chaperones can shape the evolution of viral pathogens has not been investigated.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and sets up the novelty of their work.

claim: High genetic variability is essential to support RNA virus adaptability.
source: In summary, it is clear that: (1) high genetic variability is essential to support RNA virus adaptability;
evidence: This is a summary statement based on established knowledge in virology.

claim: Missense mutations important for viral adaptation are often biophysically deleterious, constraining the accessible mutational landscape.
source: (2) missense mutations important for viral adaptation are often biophysically deleterious, constraining the accessible mutational landscape;
evidence: This is a summary statement based on established knowledge and prior citations in the manuscript.

claim: Many viruses engage host chaperones to fold their proteins.
source: and (3) many viruses engage host chaperones to fold their proteins.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on prior citations in the manuscript.

claim: TMP treatment of MDCKHSF1 cells dosably induces cHSF1 transcriptional activity in a stress-independent manner within the biologically relevant regime.
source: In these cells, termed MDCKHSF1 cells, we can dosably induce cHSF1 transcriptional activity by TMP treatment in a stress-independent manner within the biologically relevant regime (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TMP treatment of MDCKHSF1 cells provides robust access to cells expressing enhanced levels of HSF1 targets without cytotoxicity.
source: avoiding cytotoxicity that would be induced by stressors or cHSF1 overexpression and yet still providing robust access to cells expressing enhanced levels of HSF1 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: MDCKYFP cell line does not display TMP-dependent upregulation of HSF1-dependent chaperones.
source: This MDCKYFP cell line does not display TMP-dependent upregulation of HSF1-dependent chaperones, indicating that TMP induces HSF1 activity in our MDCKHSF1 cells specifically by stabilizing DHFR.cHSF1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 10 nM STA-9090 does not induce a compensatory heat shock response.
source: 10 nM STA-9090 does not induce a compensatory heat shock response (representative blot shown; N = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Influenza itself neither induces heat shock protein transcripts nor interferes with the method to activate HSF1 under the infection conditions used.
source: Importantly, monitoring chaperone levels in the context of influenza A/Wuhan/1995 (H3N2) infection shows that, under our infection conditions, influenza itself neither induces heat shock protein transcripts nor interferes with our method to activate HSF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of only 118 transcripts have expression altered ≥2 fold with a p-value <10–5 in any one or more of the treatments employed.
source: We observed a total of only 118 transcripts whose expression is altered ≥2 fold with a p-value <10–5 in any one or more of the treatments employed, indicating that we are remodeling only a small portion of the transcriptome
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Two distinctive cellular environments are created by HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition in MDCKHSF1 cells.
source: A heat map for these 118 genes highlights that two distinctive cellular environments are indeed created by HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition in MDCKHSF1 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only two transcripts meet the cutoffs (≥2 fold change, p-value <10–5) upon TMP treatment in MDCKYFP cells.
source: Moreover, only two transcripts meet these cutoffs upon TMP treatment in MDCKYFP cells, confirming that the remodeled proteostasis environment upon TMP treatment of MDCKHSF1 cells is specifically due to HSF1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Stress-independent HSF1 activation upregulates numerous classic heat shock response genes including HSP70, BAG3, HSP90AA1, DNAJB1, and FKBP4.
source: As expected, stress-independent HSF1 activation upregulates numerous classic heat shock response genes (Ryno et al., 2014), including HSP70, BAG3, HSP90AA1, DNAJB1, and FKBP4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Ryno et al., 2014.

claim: Remodeling of the cellular proteostasis network by HSF1 activation is limited to nuclear and cytosolic proteostasis mechanisms, as ER proteostasis network components are not induced.
source: This remodeling of the cellular proteostasis network is limited to nuclear and cytosolic proteostasis mechanisms, as ER proteostasis network components are not induced by TMP treatment of the MDCKHSF1 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transcript-level proteostasis network remodeling is not observed upon STA-9090 treatment, with the exception of a 2.2-fold induction of HSPB1.
source: Moreover, transcript-level proteostasis network remodeling is not observed upon STA-9090 treatment, with the exception of a 2.2-fold induction of HSPB1, as expected given the low concentration of inhibitor employed.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: HSF1 activation modestly upregulates several transcripts involved in transcription factor regulation and DNA damage, such as CAMK1, RELB, and PARP3.
source: We observe modest upregulation of several transcripts involved in transcription factor regulation and DNA damage upon HSF1 activation, such as CAMK1, RELB, and PARP3, consistent with the intimate role of HSF1 in cytoprotection (Morimoto and Santoro, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and citation to Morimoto and Santoro, 1998.

claim: STA-9090 slightly upregulates several interferon response-related transcripts, including OAS2 and MX2 (2.9 and 2.2 fold-change, respectively).
source: STA-9090 slightly upregulates several interferon response-related transcripts, including OAS2 and MX2 (2.9 and 2.2 fold-change, respectively), a phenomenon that has been previously reported upon treatment with other Hsp90 inhibitors (Yang et al., 2006; Donzé et al., 2001; Shang and Tomasi, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and citations to Yang et al., 2006; Donzé et al., 2001; Shang and Tomasi, 2006.

claim: The MOI did not vary systematically between the three distinctive proteostasis environments during serial passaging.
source: Importantly, infectious titering at intermittent passages confirmed that the MOI did not vary systematically between the three distinctive proteostasis environments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Differences observed in evolutionary trajectories cannot be attributed to either systematically altered rates of viral growth in the three different host proteostasis environments or to gross differences in cell health.
source: Thus, differences observed in evolutionary trajectories cannot be attributed to either systematically altered rates of viral growth in the three different host proteostasis environments studied here or to gross differences in cell health.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MOI and titer data showing no systematic differences between environments.

claim: Non-synonymous mutations are selected against in all folding environments, as indicated by a Dn/Ds < 1 throughout serial passaging.
source: As expected, non-synonymous mutations are selected against in all folding environments, as indicated by a Dn/Ds < 1 throughout our serial passaging (Figure 3D) (Breen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Breen et al., 2012.

claim: Non-synonymous mutations fix latest in the Hsp90-inhibited environment and earliest in the HSF1-activated environment.
source: Non-synonymous mutations fix latest in the Hsp90-inhibited environment and earliest in the HSF1-activated environment (Figure 4A; outlined in green).
evidence: This claim is supported by site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the Hsp90-inhibited environment, no mutations have exceeded 60% frequency by passage 9 or 80% frequency by passage 11.
source: For instance, in the Hsp90-inhibited environment, no mutations have exceeded 60% frequency by passage 9 or 80% frequency by passage 11.
evidence: This claim is supported by site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the HSF1-activated environment, mutations exceed 80% frequency as early as passage 9 and become fixed (>90%) by passage 11.
source: In contrast, in the HSF1-activated environment, mutations exceed 80% frequency as early as passage 9 and become fixed (>90%) by passage 11.
evidence: This claim is supported by site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: By passage 11, the shape of the non-synonymous SFS for influenza evolved in the Hsp90-inhibited environment is significantly different from that of influenza evolved in the basal and HSF1-activated environments.
source: Indeed, by passage 11, the first passage at which we observe fixed mutations in any environment, the shape of the non-synonymous SFS for influenza evolved in the Hsp90-inhibited environment is significantly different from that of influenza evolved in the basal and HSF1-activated environments (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) of site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Synonymous mutations for each environment have similar SFS within each passage.
source: We find that synonymous mutations for each environment have similar SFS within each passage, and that the Mann-Whitney test cannot distinguish between the synonymous SFS in different proteostasis environments at any stage of the serial passaging experiment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Specific synonymous mutations do not fix reproducibly in one particular environment.
source: Moreover, unlike non-synonymous mutations (see below and also see Figure 4—source data 1), specific synonymous mutations do not fix reproducibly in one particular environment (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: The host proteostasis-based perturbations of HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition primarily affect influenza evolution by modulating protein-level folding/function.
source: This observation is consistent with our expectation that, although the influenza genome does undergo selection at the RNA level (Air et al., 1990), the host proteostasis-based perturbations of HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition should primarily affect influenza evolution by modulating protein-level folding/function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that synonymous mutations show similar patterns across environments while non-synonymous mutations differ, and is supported by citation to Air et al., 1990.

claim: There is little effect of host proteostasis on strongly deleterious mutations, as illustrated by the similar Dn/Ds ratios across environments.
source: On the one hand, there is little effect on strongly deleterious mutations, as illustrated by the similar Dn/Ds ratios across environments (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rate of adaptation by accumulation of advantageous mutations is significantly reduced in the Hsp90-inhibited environment, as compared to the basal and HSF1-activated environments.
source: On the other hand, the rate of adaptation by accumulation of advantageous mutations is significantly reduced in the Hsp90-inhibited environment, as compared to the basal and HSF1-activated environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by site frequency spectra data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Residues 590–640 of polymerase PA comprise a mutational hotspot present in every host environment.
source: For example, in polymerase PA, residues 590–640 comprise a mutational hotspot present in every host environment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eight mutations occur in the N-terminal 100 residues of PB1 in the HSF1-activated environment, two mutations in the baseline environment, and only one mutation in the Hsp90-inhibited environment.
source: For example, we observe eight mutations in the N-terminal 100 residues of PB1 in the HSF1-activated environment, two mutations in the baseline environment, and only one mutation in the Hsp90-inhibited environment (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Residues 9–13 of PB1 span the loop portion of a helix-loop-helix motif that critically defines the interface with PA.
source: In particular, residues 9–13 of PB1 span the loop portion of a helix-loop-helix motif (Figure 5B, secondary structure; SS) that critically defines the interface (Figure 5C, purple) with PA (Figure 5C, red) (Reich et al., 2014; Perez and Donis, 2001; Obayashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5B-C and citations to Reich et al., 2014; Perez and Donis, 2001; Obayashi et al., 2008.

claim: PA variants that occur in both the HSF1-activated and Hsp90-inhibited environments have slightly less favorable binding energy with wild-type PB1N.
source: We observed that the PA variants, which occur in both the HSF1-activated and Hsp90-inhibited environments, have slightly less favorable binding energy with wild-type PB1N (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PB1 variants that occur exclusively in the HSF1-activated environment are destabilizing, with the K11E substitution very strongly destabilizing the PA-PB1 complex.
source: The PB1 variants, which occur exclusively in the HSF1-activated environment, are also destabilizing, with the K11E substitution very strongly destabilizing the complex (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-occurrence of certain PA variants (e.g., E629K in PA) can compensate for the strongly destabilizing effects of observed PB1 substitutions (e.g., K11E in PB1).
source: We note that co-occurrence of certain PA variants (e.g., E629K in PA) can compensate for the strongly destabilizing effects of observed PB1 substitutions (e.g., the combination of E629K in PA and K11E in PB1 results in a stable complex; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Host proteostasis impacts the fitness of destabilizing amino acid substitutions in influenza proteins in a protein-specific manner.
source: Cumulatively, these observations indicate that host proteostasis impacts the fitness of destabilizing amino acid substitutions in influenza proteins in a protein-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of proteostasis perturbations on PA versus PB1 variants.

claim: Three HA variants (N144T, V242I, and M246I) present at 20% frequency in the founder virus become fixed by passage 19 in all replicates of the HSF1-activated and basal environments, but in only one replicate of the Hsp90-inhibited environment.
source: In HA, three variants (N144T, V242I, and M246I) present at 20% frequency in our founder virus become fixed by passage 19 in all replicates of the HSF1-activated and basal environments, but in only one replicate of the Hsp90-inhibited environment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational trajectory data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The three HA variants (N144T, V242I, and M246I) completely fall out of two replicates of the Hsp90-inhibited environment by passage 9.
source: Moreover, these variants completely fall out of two replicates of the Hsp90-inhibited environment by passage 9.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational trajectory data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The three HA mutations (N144T, V242I, and M246I) occur in the globular head domain of HA that binds cellular sialic acid and has inherently high mutational tolerance.
source: The three mutations occur in the globular head domain of HA that binds cellular sialic acid and has inherently high mutational tolerance (Thyagarajan and Bloom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thyagarajan and Bloom, 2014.

claim: The PA H452Q variant is present at 20% frequency in the founder virus and becomes fixed in two replicates of the Hsp90-inhibited environment.
source: In PA, we observed that the H452Q variant is present at 20% frequency in the founder virus and becomes fixed in two replicates of the Hsp90-inhibited environment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational trajectory data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The PA H452Q variant does not become fixed in the basal environment, and is selected against in the HSF1-activated environment.
source: This variant does not become fixed in the basal environment, and is selected against in the HSF1-activated environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational trajectory data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The H452Q mutation is known to occur preferentially in reassorted viruses compared to pure strains, which is indicative of a fitness cost.
source: Interestingly, although the H452Q mutation is far from the PA endonuclease site, (Reich et al., 2014) it is known to occur preferentially in reassorted viruses compared to pure strains, which is indicative of a fitness cost (Zeldovich et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reich et al., 2014 and Zeldovich et al., 2015.

claim: Hsp90 inhibition significantly enhances the fitness of the H452Q PA variant relative to wild-type PA, while HSF1 activation significantly reduces it.
source: We found that Hsp90 inhibition does indeed significantly enhance the fitness of the H452Q variant relative to wild-type PA, while HSF1 activation significantly reduces it (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse genetics competition experiment data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: H452Q PA has a predicted ΔΔG of +1.10 kcal/mol relative to wild-type PA.
source: One likely possibility is that Hsp90 delays subunit assembly or directs destabilized PA variants to degradation, as H452Q has a predicted ΔΔG of +1.10 kcal/mol relative to wild-type PA (Yin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction using Eris, cited as Yin et al., 2007.

claim: Prior to this work, the possibility that host chaperones significantly modulate pathogen evolution had not been rigorously investigated.
source: However, prior to this work, the possibility that host chaperones significantly modulate pathogen evolution had not been rigorously investigated.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and establishes the novelty of their work.

claim: Two unique proteostasis perturbations, HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition, have distinctive consequences for client protein evolution.
source: Moreover, in eukaryotic systems, research has focused largely on Hsp90 inhibition. Here, we not only define a new role for host proteostasis in influenza evolution, but we also show that two unique proteostasis perturbations, HSF1 activation and Hsp90 inhibition, have distinctive consequences for client protein evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Non-synonymous mutations are fixed more slowly when Hsp90 is inhibited and more quickly when HSF1 is activated.
source: At the whole genome-level, our data indicate that non-synonymous mutations are fixed more slowly when Hsp90 is inhibited and more quickly when HSF1 is activated.
evidence: This claim is supported by site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overall shape of the Hsp90-inhibited passage 11 SFS is significantly different from that observed in the other two environments.
source: Moreover, the overall shape of the Hsp90-inhibited passage 11 SFS is significantly different from that observed in the other two environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of site frequency spectra data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Moderately destabilizing variants in PA are tolerated in all three host proteostasis environments studied.
source: Interestingly, moderately destabilizing variants in PA are tolerated in all three host proteostasis environments studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis and molecular dynamics data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Amino acid substitutions in the N-terminus of PB1 are observed only when HSF1 is activated.
source: In contrast, amino acid substitutions in the N-terminus of PB1 are observed only when HSF1 is activated.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PB1 variants strongly destabilize the PB1:PA complex and thus may be accessible only in host cells with high chaperone levels.
source: These PB1 variants strongly destabilize the PB1:PA complex and thus may be accessible only in host cells with high chaperone levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from molecular dynamics data and the observation that these variants only appear in HSF1-activated environments.

claim: Polymerase assembly is known to be mediated by cytosolic host chaperones.
source: Indeed, polymerase assembly is known to be mediated by cytosolic host chaperones (Naito et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Naito et al., 2007.

claim: The evolution of the influenza polymerase complex may be modulated by host proteostasis in significant ways.
source: These observations indicate that the evolution of the influenza polymerase complex may be modulated by host proteostasis in significant ways.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing differential mutational tolerance at the PA-PB1 interface in different proteostasis environments.

claim: Host proteostasis impacts the fitness of specific mutations in at least two viral proteins (PA and HA).
source: At the level of individual mutations, our data demonstrate that host proteostasis impacts the fitness of specific mutations in at least two viral proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational trajectory and reverse genetics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The directionality of the effect of host proteostasis on mutation fitness seems to be specific to a given variant or protein.
source: Intriguingly, the directionality of this effect seems to be specific to a given variant or protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PA H452Q and HA variants respond differently to proteostasis perturbations.

claim: The apparently destabilizing H452Q PA variant is significantly more fit when Hsp90 is inhibited, but significantly less fit when HSF1 is activated.
source: For example, the apparently destabilizing H452Q PA variant is significantly more fit when Hsp90 is inhibited, but significantly less fit when HSF1 is activated.
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse genetics competition data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Host proteostasis modulates the nature of selection on the influenza genome, the mutational tolerance of specific influenza proteins, and the trajectories of particular variants.
source: Thus, we observe that host proteostasis modulates the nature of selection on the influenza genome, the mutational tolerance of specific influenza proteins, and the trajectories of particular variants.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The consequences of altered host proteostasis for influenza evolution are emerging in the course of a relatively short-timescale evolution experiment, and without exerting additional selection pressure such as treatment with antiviral drugs.
source: These results are especially compelling because consequences of altered host proteostasis for influenza evolution are emerging in the course of a relatively short-timescale evolution experiment, and without exerting additional selection pressure such as treatment with antiviral drugs.
evidence: This claim emphasizes the significance of the findings given the experimental design.

claim: The observations may derive from direct interactions between host proteostasis components and influenza proteins, or from indirect consequences of perturbing proteostasis.
source: As in previous studies on the role of Hsp90 in the evolution of their endogenous protein clients, our observations may derive from direct interactions between host proteostasis components and influenza proteins, or from indirect consequences of perturbing proteostasis.
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism and is speculative.

claim: This role for host proteostasis in modulating both the pace and the directionality of influenza evolution is provocative.
source: Regardless of its precise origin, this role for host proteostasis in modulating both the pace and the directionality of influenza evolution is provocative.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Defining the molecular details of the interplay between host proteostasis and viral evolution will be essential to fully elucidate the factors potentiating and constraining viral evolution.
source: Defining the molecular details of this interplay between host proteostasis and viral evolution will be essential to fully elucidate the factors potentiating and constraining viral evolution.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about future research needs.

claim: Such studies may eventually enable design of improved antiviral therapeutics and antibodies that are refractory to the evolution of resistance.
source: Moreover, such studies may eventually enable design of improved antiviral therapeutics and antibodies that are refractory to the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the research.

claim: MDCK cells were cultured at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin/streptomycin/glutamine.
source: MDCK cells were cultured at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere in DMEM (CellGro) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (CellGro) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin/glutamine (CellGro).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing cell culture conditions.

claim: All experiments were performed with influenza A/Wuhan/1995 (H3N2).
source: All experiments were performed with influenza A/Wuhan/1995 (H3N2), which was generously provided by Prof. Jianzhu Chen (MIT).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the viral strain used.

claim: Serial passaging experiments were performed on a 12-well scale in biological triplicate, at 100,000 cells/well and an MOI of 0.002 virions/cell.
source: Serial passaging experiments were performed on a 12-well scale in biological triplicate, at 100,000 cells/well and an MOI of 0.002 virions/cell, as estimated by hemagglutination titering.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the serial passaging protocol.

claim: Cells were pre-treated with TMP or DMSO for 24 hr or with STA-9090 for 90 min prior to influenza infection to establish altered proteostasis environments.
source: Cells were pre-treated with TMP or DMSO for 24 hr or with STA-9090 for 90 min prior to influenza infection to establish altered proteostasis environments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the treatment protocol.

claim: Infections were allowed to proceed for 48 hr, after which the viral supernatant was harvested, cleared of cellular debris by centrifugation, and titered using a hemagglutination assay.
source: Infections were allowed to proceed for 48 hr, after which the viral supernatant was harvested, cleared of cellular debris by centrifugation, and titered using a hemagglutination assay (Eisfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the infection and titering protocol.

claim: Only positions with greater than 600-fold coverage in all replicates of each sample were included in the analysis.
source: Only positions with greater than 600-fold coverage in all replicates of each sample were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the sequencing data analysis criteria.

claim: Variant alleles present at greater than 1.5% frequency are included in the site frequency spectra, protein alignment, and mutational trajectories analyses.
